analysis.one_liner: Adds a prescription drug benefit to Medicare and curbs tactics that delay cheaper generic drugs.
analysis.headline: The Senate Democratic leader's Medicare drug bill, introduced January 7, 2003 and referred that day to the Finance Committee, never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add a voluntary outpatient prescription drug benefit to Medicare, with a $25 monthly premium, no deductible, and a cap on yearly out-of-pocket drug costs. It would also try to lower drug prices by speeding up generic drug competition, restricting patent tactics brand-name makers use to delay generic rivals, and allowing prescription drug imports. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries without reliable drug coverage — the bill's own findings say at least two-thirds of beneficiaries have unreliable, inadequate, or no drug coverage, and that seniors without coverage pay about 15 percent more per prescription. It also helps consumers generally by making cheaper generics available sooner, and helps low-income beneficiaries through extra cost-sharing assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries and people buying prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: Creates a voluntary Medicare Part D drug benefit with a $25 monthly premium, no deductible, 50% coinsurance that stops entirely once a beneficiary's yearly out-of-pocket drug costs reach $3,700, plus extra cost-sharing assistance for low-income beneficiaries [S3][S2].

Requires drug makers to register patents with the FDA within 30 days of approval, with late registration barring later patent-infringement suits, and limits the 30-month freeze on generic approval to later-issued patents [S2][S3].
Strips the 180-day generic marketing exclusivity from a first generic applicant whose own conduct delays or prevents the generic from reaching the market [S2].
Adds provisions on importing prescription drugs from abroad and on pediatric labeling of drugs [S2][S3].
Cites Congressional Budget Office estimates that substituting generics for brand-name drugs could save purchasers $8–10 billion per year, with generics costing 25–60 percent less [S3].
Extends Medicare coverage of immunosuppressive drugs to all beneficiaries [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the benefit through a new Prescription Drug Account in the Medicare trust fund, enrollees pay the premium and 50 percent coinsurance up to the yearly cap, and brand-name drug makers bear the cost of curbed patent-delay tactics, faster generics, and importation competition.

drawbacks.text: Enrollees pay half the cost of their drugs until out-of-pocket spending reaches $3,700 in a year, so expensive drug regimens still cost thousands out of pocket before the cap kicks in [S3].

The benefit is delivered through competing private entities — insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and pharmacies — operating under federal contract, with each plan's own formulary and appeals process, rather than directly by Medicare [S3].
The premium starts at $25 a month and rises with the program's per-capita drug spending in later years [S3].

Weakening patent enforcement tools and allowing drug imports reduces the revenue stream that brand-name makers argue funds research into new drugs — the standard industry objection to this kind of cost-containment bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and well-targeted: a known premium, no deductible, and a hard cap on yearly out-of-pocket drug costs directly addresses the finding that most beneficiaries had no reliable coverage. The 50 percent coinsurance before the cap is heavy, and delivering the benefit through private contractors adds a layer between Medicare and beneficiaries. The cost-containment title (faster generics, importation) is where the biggest structural savings sit, and it is also what the brand-name industry would fight hardest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle, the Senate Democratic leader, introduced the bill on January 7, 2003 with 18 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance that same day [S1][S5][S3].
Twenty-one senators cosponsored the bill; all were Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no further action after the January 7, 2003 referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers were the clear winners: the bill's cost-containment title, which targeted the patent tactics that keep generics off the market and permitted drug imports, never got a hearing. Seniors kept waiting for a drug benefit, and the version of Medicare drug coverage that became law in late 2003 was delivered through private insurers without government price negotiation.

against.what_they_did: Fought government-run drug benefits, generic access reforms, and drug importation during the 2003 Medicare debate

sides.party_line_note: All 22 supporters — the sponsor and 21 cosponsors — were Democrats, no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill sat in a committee chaired by a Republican until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill's Title II directly targets the tools brand-name makers use to stretch market exclusivity: it forces 30-day patent registration with the FDA, limits the 30-month freeze on generic approval, and punishes delay tactics by forfeiting generic exclusivity. It also allows drug importation and requires pediatric testing, all of which cut into branded revenue at seniors' expense.
Clearing away patent-registration traps and misuse of the 30-month stay means more generics reach the market sooner, which the bill's findings tie to $8–10 billion in annual savings for purchasers.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The benefit flows through private 'eligible entities' — insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and pharmacy systems — bidding for federal contracts, making them the permanent delivery channel for a new public benefit with a guaranteed management payment.

Plans must sign participation agreements paying a dispensing fee and cannot exclude willing pharmacies, and rural pharmacists could get bonus payments, but pharmacies must stick to negotiated prices and accept audits.

industries.industry: Large employers with retiree health plans
industries.note: An employer incentive program pays sponsors two-thirds of the government's per-person contribution for each retiree kept on an employer drug plan instead of Medicare.
